name: The Bur Oak on the Midway

location.address: Midway Plaisance at Ellis Avenue, Hyde Park, Chicago, IL

access: Free, public park path along the Midway Plaisance
transport: Metra Electric District to 59th St/University of Chicago station, about 22 minutes from Millennium Station downtown, then a short walk to Ellis Ave and the Midway
verify_notes: A giant bur oak on the Midway Plaisance near Ellis Ave, in front of (west of) the University of Chicago's Billings Hospital. Hyde Park community historian Gary Ossewaarde estimated it at 250+ years old in a 2009 note (so 265+ by 2026), based on second-hand information; he flagged that a Lincoln Park oak might have been even older (that tree, at Lincoln Park Zoo, was removed in 2023, see blocked list). The tree appears in Henry C. Cowles' 1901 ecology textbook as 'THE example of its kind,' meaning it was already a substantial specimen 125+ years ago. A local history blog (Patricia Morse, 2020, with a 2024 reader comment) says a 2024 trunk-diameter measurement exceeded the largest bur oak on the Morton Arboretum's own age/growth reference chart, suggesting it could be older still. It is the one tree the Olmsted brothers' sons left standing when they cleared the Midway's original grid design for the 1893 World's Fair; some accounts place it behind the Fair's Sitting Bull's Cabin exhibit and Ostrich Farm concession. SOURCE CONFLICT for the writer to handle, not resolve silently: a University of Chicago Magazine piece quotes campus environment official Richard Bumstead describing this same tree ('a giant bur oak... on the Midway, in front of the hospital') as having been 'ostensibly planted as part of a Native American exhibit during the...1893' World's Fair, which contradicts the multiple sources saying it long predates the fair and was deliberately spared. State both versions, or lead with the better-sourced pre-fair account (Cowles 1901, Ossewaarde, Morse) and note the magazine's competing claim. Tree removals reported at Midway Plaisance in Feb 2024 were at the EAST end near Jackson Park (a playground/landscape redesign), unrelated to this tree at the west end near Ellis Ave.

name: The Bur Oak Grove of Wooded Island
age_estimate: the grove's oldest survivors are roughly 200 to 300 years

location.address: Wooded Island, Jackson Park, south end near the Clarence Darrow Bridge and Osaka Garden (6200 S. Cornell Ave area), Chicago, IL

access: Free, public park, Chicago Park District (Wooded Island / Osaka Garden)
transport: Metra Electric District to 59th St/University of Chicago station, about 22 minutes from downtown, then roughly a 15 to 20 minute walk east across Jackson Park to Wooded Island; or CTA bus to the Museum of Science and Industry and cross the Clarence Darrow Bridge
verify_notes: A cluster of bur oaks on the south end of Wooded Island in Jackson Park, part of the Frederick Law Olmsted-designed 1893 World's Fair landscape (Wooded Island was the one part of the fairgrounds deliberately kept free of buildings, natural throughout). DNAinfo (2016) reported 250-year-old bur oaks on the island alongside a 150-year-old red oak; a separate bur oak that blew down around 2016 was counted back to a start date around 1730 (nearly 300 years old when it fell), suggesting the survivors are of similar vintage. The Hyde Park Herald piece contrasts the oaks' view (favored by fair-era artists) against the formal Court of Honor to the south, and describes the island as preserving an undisturbed sand-ridge soil structure that local naturalists date back thousands of years (that is an ecosystem/soil claim, not a claim about any one tree's age). The Army Corps of Engineers' 2016, $8.1M habitat restoration explicitly preserved the existing bur oaks and 120 naturally-sprouted bur oak saplings growing around them (volunteer steward Jerry Levy is quoted and would be a good contact for a future photo pass). Reachable via the Clarence Darrow Bridge (Darrow reportedly practiced oratory speeches from it); Osaka Garden sits at the island's north end, the oak grove at the south end nearer the old Court of Honor site. This is a grove/ensemble entry rather than one named tree: recommend the writer describe the view from the path just south of Osaka Garden as the one place to stand.

name: The Bur Oak Savanna of Union Ridge Cemetery
age_estimate: the oldest estimated at 325 to 375 years, based on trunk size

location.address: Union Ridge Cemetery, 6700 W Higgins Ave, Chicago, IL 60656

access: Free, cemetery grounds open to visitors during posted hours
transport: Metra Union Pacific Northwest Line to Norwood Park station, about 22 minutes from Ogilvie Transportation Center downtown, then a short walk
verify_notes: A small savanna of mature bur oaks stands in the oldest section of Union Ridge Cemetery, first used for burial in 1841 and described by the Norwood Park Historical Society as Chicago's oldest continuously operating cemetery. DNAinfo (2016) cites an expert, Scott Carlini, estimating the oldest of the grove at 325 to 375 years old based on trunk diameter; no ring core was taken, so this is a size-based estimate, flag accordingly. The cemetery grounds sat on open prairie before being platted, which fits a relict bur oak stand (bur oak is the classic fire- and drought-tolerant species of the tallgrass prairie edge in this region), and the cemetery's own history page corroborates the founding date and prairie setting. CAUTION: only one named source (Carlini) is quoted on the specific age figure across everything found in this pass; a second, independent numeric estimate was not located, so the age claim is directional rather than doubly confirmed and should stay flagged until a second source turns up. Exact coordinates of the specific oldest tree within the grounds were not found; the pin here is the cemetery gate/office, an honest approximate. It is a functioning cemetery, so note standard visiting-hours access rather than open-park access in the story.
